C1.justification: V2 reframes the contributions around systematic failure of existing Gaussian methods, a transient-flame formulation, and a combined appearance/depth/motion/video evaluation protocol. The introduction makes broader claims about existing methods being unable to reconstruct fire reliably. The abstract extends validation to simulated fire, and the conclusion emphasizes improved motion alignment and depth consistency.

C2.justification: V2 adds a causal account involving persistent primitives, geometric absorption, depth collapse and temporal drift, plus interpretations of masking and joint optimization as physical-versus-visual tradeoffs. Appendix B newly argues that explicit shutter modeling is unnecessary at the tested motion speeds. The main limitations remain largely unchanged. One new interpretation is inconsistent: page 9 says separating optimization improves simulation performance, whereas Table 2 slightly favors JointOpt.

D1.justification: V2 substantially revises implementation documentation, adding alpha-loss rendering details, scale constraints, camera orientation, simulation construction, and the unofficial FreeTimeGS implementation and initialization procedure. V1's background-sphere initialization and Yang baseline Gaussian-cap/checkpoint-selection descriptions disappear, without establishing that those settings were changed. Appendix I replaces bundled-example and future-release directions with an official repository link. Hardware and the proposed method's training budgets remain unchanged.

E1.justification: V2 retains the 17 real-world fire scenes and adds synthetic fire reconstruction in the classroom, junkshop and monk environments. These Mantaflow/Blender scenes introduce a simulated domain with known volumetric velocities, substantially extending coverage beyond real videos with estimated depth.

E2.justification: The real-world comparison expands from the Wu and Yang 4DGS methods to include Grid4D and FreeTimeGS (Table 1). FreeTimeGS was already cited as a methodological foundation in v1, but was not an evaluated comparator. All four baselines also participate in the new motion and video-quality comparisons.

E3.justification: The two 4DGS baselines change from reported random initialization to COLMAP initialization. V2 introduces density-weighted volumetric evaluation and full-video CGVQM with soft masking of synchronization hardware. Synthetic evaluation uses 50 frames per camera over two seconds and 640-cubed velocity grids. NoSync changes from v1's one-frame or up-to-one-frame offsets to half-frame offsets; the real-data every-eighth-frame holdout remains unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds the NoMask ablation, evaluates component effects on simulated motion, and introduces a RoMa matching-failure analysis (Figure 12). It removes the quantitative GlobalShutter ablation and detailed per-scene ablation tables, although Appendix B retains the finding that explicit shutter handling did not improve image metrics. These changes substantially revise the evidence about component roles and failure mechanisms.

E5.justification: V1 explicitly identifies Table 1 entries as means and standard deviations across scenes. V2 retains the plus-or-minus format but omits that explicit definition, including for its new motion and video metrics. Neither version documents repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or formal significance tests; additional result rows do not establish additional runs.

E6.justification: Real-world results are extensively replaced: the proposed method's flame PSNR changes from 27.46 to 26.93, full-image PSNR from 33.61 to 35.89, and depth RMSE from 0.0412 to 0.094. The full-image ranking changes from Yang 4DGS leading to the proposed method leading. Settings also change, preventing interpretation as controlled performance gains. New results include motion cosine similarity of 0.744 and CGVQM of 86.1; per-scene baseline and ablation results are removed.

M1.justification: The two-stage, flow-initialized Gaussian model retains its lifetime and constant-velocity equations. V2 adds a motion-mask opacity loss weighted by 0.1 and bounds dynamic Gaussian scales using a voxel-scaled sigmoid (Section 3.2; Appendix H). Rolling-shutter modeling is presented as an optional extension. These refine the existing procedure rather than replace its core representation.

P1.justification: The introduction and contribution narrative are extensively rewritten, with substantial revisions to results interpretation and methodological explanations. Rolling-shutter treatment moves from the main methodology to Appendix B. The supplement is reorganized from Sections 8–14 into thematic Appendices A–J, with reordered dataset, implementation, visualization and resource sections.

P2.justification: Comparison figures are redesigned for four baselines, and new motion visualizations, synthetic-scene montages and a RoMa matching illustration are added. Existing fire-removal and capture-setup images move to the appendix. Real-world comparisons and ablations merge into a color-highlighted table, with new motion and video tables. Six per-scene baseline/ablation tables and the rolling-shutter illustration are removed; retained dataset and per-scene tables are reformatted.

R1.justification: Positioning shifts from a FreeTimeGS-based reconstruction pipeline toward a transient-Gaussian formulation claimed to overcome general failures of existing Gaussian representations. V2 also introduces an efficiency-based rationale for excluding non-Gaussian comparisons. It adds references to RoMa, Grid4D, CGVQM+D and MotionGS and removes R3D3; the broad related-work survey is otherwise largely retained.

T1.justification: V2 Section 3.4 adds mathematical definitions for density-weighted motion comparison: opacity-volume weights, expected ground-truth velocities approximated by Gauss-Hermite quadrature, and weighted relative L2 and cosine scores. It also removes duplicated depth-loss weighting from the displayed formulation. Existing flow-reconstruction and rolling-shutter derivations are substantially retained; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation of the central motion-reconstruction claim. V1 relied on image metrics, monocular-depth proxies and qualitative evidence; v2 adds direct comparison with simulated ground-truth velocities, video-quality evaluation and two additional baselines with better-documented initialization. This addresses an important evidential gap rather than merely increasing reported performance. The gains outweigh the loss of detailed per-scene comparisons, less explicit uncertainty labeling, and remaining weaknesses in the broad baseline-failure claims and contradictory JointOpt interpretation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Gaussians on Fire and contain readable main texts, equations, figures, tables and supplementary material. Content can be matched across the substantial reorganization, supporting a reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 reports original real-world reconstruction experiments, adds three simulated fire scenes with ground-truth velocity evaluation, and reports video-quality results.

before.justification: V1 reports original reconstruction experiments on 17 captured fire scenes, including baseline comparisons, component ablations and per-scene results.

results.title: Gaussians on Fire: High-Frequency Reconstruction of Flames

C1.justification: The abstract replaces the blanket statement that Wid3R consistently outperforms prior methods with metric- and dataset-specific gains, and explicitly claims benefits from diverse-camera conditioning under sparse 360-degree supervision. The contribution bullets clarify multi-view novelty. The central reconstruction contributions and conclusion remain intact.

C2.justification: The supplement explains the attention choice through degradation with angular-radial cross-attention, expands the efficiency and calibration arguments against cubemap preprocessing, and proposes geometric guidance for scene generation while acknowledging that integration remains future work. The existing limitation concerning dynamic scenes is unchanged.

D1.justification: V2 substantially expands reproducibility information with dataset counts, uniform dataset sampling, softmin pseudocode, token/attention wiring, and a project-page link. However, Table 4 replaces exact localization scene identifiers with generic labels. Supplementary Table 1 also implies approximately 4.1% spherical training images, conflicting with the retained main-text claim of less than 1%.

E1.justification: The training datasets and established evaluation benchmarks remain unchanged. Supplementary Section 1 and Figure 1 add a qualitative reconstruction test on synthesized images from panorama-based scene generation, extending the input domain without demonstrating an integrated generation system.

E2.justification: Tables 2, 3, and 5 add Ours (π3), fine-tuned on the paper's training data, substantially strengthening the central comparisons. Supplementary Figure 4 adds cubemap-to-π3 inference. Main Figure 4 removes SPSG+COLMAP from its qualitative comparison, although Table 4 retains it.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce a training-data-matched π3 control, attention variants, and a cubemap procedure converting 37 spherical images into 222 perspective images. Existing benchmark splits, metrics, image resolution, and alignment procedures remain unchanged. Supplementary dataset counts disclose settings rather than establish changed sample sizes.

E4.justification: V2 adds substantial tests of the architectural rationale: fine-tuned π3 examines benefits beyond training-data adaptation, and supplementary Table 3 compares cross-attention with self-attention. Cubemap reconstruction, predicted-ray visualizations, and additional reconstruction cases expand diagnostic evidence. The original Table 7 ablations remain unchanged.

E5.justification: Table 7 retains the same standard-deviation reporting, and Stanford2D3D retains ten sampling repetitions per scene and twenty cases. No new seed information, repeated-training-run counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported.

E6.justification: Existing main-table scores are retained, but substantial new results alter comparative rankings. In Table 2, fine-tuned π3 achieves FIORD AUC@30 of 72.56 versus Wid3R's 68.20, while Stanford2D3D scores are 62.14 versus 79.93. Supplementary Table 3 adds attention results, including Stanford2D3D mean accuracy error of 0.273 for cross-attention versus 0.197 for self-attention, alongside new qualitative findings.

M1.justification: The ray-based angular/radial architecture, camera tokens, pose prediction, and training losses remain unchanged. Supplementary Sections 3–5 disclose sampling and attention details, including radial self-attention; they do not establish a revision of v1's implemented method.

P1.justification: The abstract and selected introductory and related-work paragraphs are rewritten, method subsection titles are refined, and a separately organized supplement expands explanations. The main method–experiments–conclusion structure and much of its prose remain unchanged.

P2.justification: The supplement adds architecture, ray, generation, and cubemap diagrams, data and attention tables, pseudocode, and extensive qualitative panels. Main Table 1 is redesigned around distortion awareness, Figure 4 is redrawn with fewer comparator columns, and Tables 2, 3, and 5 accommodate the additional baseline.

R1.justification: V2 adds Depth Anything 3 and MapAnything to the ray-representation discussion, clarifies distinctions from calibration-token methods and UniK3D, and cites panorama/world-generation work for the supplementary application. These extend the context while retaining the central positioning around distortion-aware multi-view reconstruction.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation and Equations 1–12 remain unchanged. Supplementary sampling pseudocode elaborates the existing proximity-based sampler; no new theorem, proof, substantive derivation, or formal assumption is introduced.

improvement.justification: The training-data-matched π3 comparison addresses an important weakness in v1: separating architectural benefits from adaptation to wide-angle training data. Together with the attention ablation and detailed sampling/architecture disclosures, it substantially strengthens validation and reproducibility, including revealing FIORD exceptions to Wid3R's advantage. Lost localization scene identifiers and inconsistent spherical-data counts are reporting regressions, but their localized impact is outweighed by these substantive evidentiary gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Wid3R and provide readable text, equations, tables, and figures. V1 ends after its references; v2 adds a seven-page supplement. The supplied material supports comparison throughout.

after.justification: V2 retains those experiments and adds fine-tuned baseline results, an attention ablation, and qualitative cubemap and synthesized-scene evaluations.

before.justification: V1 reports original pose, localization, point-map, and monocular-depth experiments, plus training-data and camera-token ablations in Tables 2–7.

results.title: Wid3R: Wide Field-of-View 3D Reconstruction via Camera Model Conditioning

C1.justification: The central contributions remain compact Gaussian initialization and gradient-free recurrent refinement. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion extend the generalization claim explicitly to unseen view counts, while the stated empirical scope expands to ACID and 32-view inputs.

C2.justification: v2 adds mechanism explanations concerning middle-view coordinate alignment, hidden-state features, weight-sharing regularization, and DINOv2's spatial limitations. It also discusses the narrowing advantage over optimization with more views. The limitations retain computational bottlenecks but remove v1's conjecture that fixed Gaussian counts cause iteration saturation.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies two-layer Gaussian and four-layer update heads, the middle-view coordinate reference, and details of additional baseline adaptations. These disclosures do not establish changes to previously unspecified implementations. Training budgets are relocated unchanged, and code release remains prospective. Table 1 removes the explicit single-GH200 timing-hardware statement.

E1.justification: v2 adds zero-shot RealEstate10K-to-ACID evaluation (Table 4) and generalization from eight training views to unseen input-view counts (Figure 5b). Appendix A also evaluates expanded scene coverage with up to 32 views. These substantially broaden the tested generalization scenarios beyond v1.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated SplatFormer (Table 10), 3DGS refinement initialized by ReSplat (Table 8), and depth-regularized 3DGS (Table 11), substantially expanding relevant alternatives. The cited sparse-view optimization papers motivate the depth-regularized comparator; their named methods are not separately reported as evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: Training samples one to four recurrent iterations instead of one to three. New experimental designs control initialization for refinement comparisons, vary weight sharing and network depth, and expand the sampling region and target-view coverage across view counts (Tables 7-9). Existing progressive training schedules and budgets are retained in Appendix B.

E4.justification: v2 expands rendering-error ablations to RGB, feature, and fusion alternatives, and adds coordinate-system, hidden-state, weight-sharing/depth, feature-extractor, and component-runtime analyses (Tables 6, 9, 12, and 13). View-count robustness and qualitative ablations are also added. The original compression and initialization ablations remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, experimental seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Additional result tables retain the same point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: Reported recurrent results change substantially: Table 1's three-iteration PSNR changes from 26.82 to 27.65, with a new four-iteration result of 27.70. Table 2's two-iteration PSNR changes from 23.23 to 23.51, and Table 3 from 29.72 to 29.75. These accompany model/training revisions. ACID, new comparators, and expanded analyses add many results; compression and initialization-ablation values remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Section 3.2 changes the feedback signal from ResNet-feature residuals alone to their sum with projected RGB residuals, using pixel unshuffle, a linear layer, and LayerNorm. This modifies one component while retaining compact initialization, attention-based recurrent updates, and the training losses.

P1.justification: The main section order and much of the narrative remain intact. Local passages are rewritten, training details move to Appendix B, and the appendix gains separate evaluation, visualization, and LLM-use sections. The acknowledgments are removed; the expansion primarily documents added scientific content.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands tables and plots, rebuilds Figure 3 with rendering-error heatmaps and per-image PSNR, adds a view-count generalization panel, and introduces iteration and ablation visualizations. Existing compression and Gaussian-reconstruction images are retained and relocated: v1 Figures 6-8 become v2 Figures 7, 12, and 13.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for LayerNorm, COLMAP, ACID, and two sparse-view optimization works, and expands its discussion of SplatFormer's scene-level adaptation difficulties. The main related-work organization and positioning against single-step reconstruction and gradient-based refinement remain.

T1.justification: v2 Equation 5 revises the mathematical definition of rendering-error feedback to combine feature residuals with projected RGB residuals. The remaining update and loss mathematics is retained apart from notation and numbering; neither version supplies theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important gaps in evidence for recurrent refinement: Table 8 controls initialization, while Table 9 compares weight sharing against stacked and deeper alternatives. Expanded mechanism ablations and generalization tests substantially strengthen support for the central contribution. These gains outweigh limited reporting problems, including Table 8's 0.960 SSIM entry conflicting with its best-value highlighting and the removed timing-hardware disclosure.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ReSplat with the same authors, core approach, and retained experiments. Text, equations, tables, figures, and all appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports revised original experiments and additional ACID evaluation, controlled refinement comparisons, architectural ablations, and runtime analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original view-synthesis experiments on DL3DV and RealEstate10K, generalization tests, ablations, and reconstructed-scene visualizations.

results.title: ReSplat: Learning Recurrent Gaussian Splatting

C1.justification: v1 claims state-of-the-art performance across retrieval/localization and point-cloud understanding. v2’s abstract, contribution list, and conclusion reserve that claim for point-cloud understanding and describe retrieval/localization as competitive. The conclusion also adds a 90% total-processing-time reduction claim. Figure 1 and Appendix C retain broader state-of-the-art wording.

C2.justification: New Section 6 identifies limited upsampled-feature resolution, difficulty with small or crowded objects, and lack of real-time novel-view feature rendering. Sections 4.4–4.5 newly attribute advantages to dense registration beyond encoder choice and explain memory costs through mask-proposal caching. These materially expand the mechanism discussion and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v2 specifies chunking and FP16 for Dr. Splat’s previously mentioned memory optimization, discloses SAM-level and filtering choices, and gives image counts for memory measurements. Conversely, it removes v1’s explicit softmax and weighted vertex-score aggregation description from Section 4.3; this omission does not establish a changed implementation.

E1.justification: Appendix D/Table 10 adds 200-class ScanNet200 evaluation, extending semantic-category coverage within the existing indoor point-cloud understanding task. LERF retrieval/localization, ScanNet 10/15/19-class evaluation, and KITTI-360 segmentation/editing coverage are retained.

E2.justification: v2 adds LaGa to LERF 3D and ScanNet comparisons, Occam’s LGS to LERF 2D comparison, and both to the runtime comparison. Appendix Table 10 newly compares OpenVoxel on ScanNet19; its ScanNet200 entries are blank. The backbone ablation also newly evaluates Dr. Splat with AM-RADIO.

E3.justification: Added experiments introduce a separate multi-level-SAM LaGa setting, representation-by-encoder controls, and per-scene peak-memory measurement. Existing benchmark metrics and feature-transfer settings are retained. Newly stated SAM-level and mean-filtering details clarify existing evaluations without establishing that those experiments were changed or rerun.

E4.justification: v1’s sequential LERF ablation is expanded into geometry ablations on LERF and ScanNet and a crossed representation/backbone comparison in v2 Tables 4–5. These test whether improvements arise from geometry, encoder choice, or their combination. Table 6 adds memory analysis. Existing upsampling and TSDF analyses remain in Appendices A–B.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Reported averages aggregate benchmark results; geometric confidence weights are not statistical uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Existing LESV benchmark scores are retained, but substantial results are added for competitors, ablations, memory, and ScanNet200. Table 10 reports ScanNet200 mIoU/mAcc of 30.65/42.35 for LESV versus 17.88/25.96 for Dr. Splat. Table 6 reports average peak memory of 22.5 versus 131.75 GB. New ablation tables give Dr. Splat LERF mIoU as 52.76, inconsistent with the retained 52.67 in Table 1.

M1.justification: Equation 9 removes the +epsilon stabilizer from the sliding-window aggregation denominator, a small change to the specified normalization. The SVRaster backbone, geometric losses, TSDF confidence fusion, AM-RADIO features, SCRA/SCGA, and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. An implementation change beyond this formula edit is not established.

P1.justification: Targeted rewrites affect related work, evaluation explanations, ablation and efficiency discussions, and the conclusion. A limitations section and ScanNet200 appendix section are added, and the unresolved Figure ?? reference becomes Figure 5. The overall narrative organization and most method and existing appendix text remain recognizable.

P2.justification: v2 restructures the ablation display, adds backbone, memory, and ScanNet200 tables, and expands existing comparison tables. Figures 1–10 retain their visual content, with relocation and reflow. The page canvas and margins change, while the basic figure and table design is preserved.

R1.justification: v2 expands positioning to multi-view consensus, contrastive grouping, and the closely related voxel-based OpenVoxel approach. It adds Beyond Averages, LaGa, Occam’s LGS, OpenVoxel, and Trace3D, with substantive discussion of their relationship to LESV. The J-NeuS reference and its attribution in the depth-confidence discussion are removed.

T1.justification: Equation 9’s mathematical definition changes by removing the denominator epsilon. Other mathematical formulations and the multi-level TSDF algorithm are retained, apart from notation and punctuation edits. No new theorem, proof, or formal assumption is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the central contribution: Tables 4–5 address the representation-versus-encoder attribution gap in v1, while memory measurements and additional competitors better test its efficiency and accuracy claims. Narrowed headline claims and concrete limitations improve calibration. Some scoring documentation is lost, and numerical inconsistencies and overly broad claims remain, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the stronger experimental support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LESV research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and can be matched despite reflow, renumbering, and additions.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds backbone controls, memory measurements, baseline comparisons, and ScanNet200 results.

before.justification: v1 reports original LERF retrieval, ScanNet segmentation, ablation, and runtime results, plus KITTI-360 demonstrations in the appendix.

results.title: LESV:Language Embedded Sparse Voxel Fusion for Open-Vocabulary 3D Scene Understanding

C1.justification: The central alignment, distillation, and boundary contributions remain. v3 narrows the blanket absence-of-2D-supervision claim to no pretrained 2D features or language supervision in the segmentation pipeline, drops the 'first approach' claim, and replaces overall state-of-the-art assertions with competitive-performance claims. Opacity's contribution is specified more precisely as visibility cues.

C2.justification: v3 develops opacity as structural/visibility confidence, explains why SH and rotation are excluded, and acknowledges texture-induced small-scale boundary noise. It adds interpretations of reconstruction-quality dependence and geometry-versus-appearance tradeoffs. Sections A and E explicitly discuss offline preparation costs, Gaussian availability, and outdoor scale variability, substantially extending v2's brief indoor-coverage qualification.

D1.justification: v3 supplies teacher batch size and learning rate, B–S channel dimensions and attention heads, boundary-head architecture, explicit training-only split usage, and the nearest-Gaussian fallback. It specifies the 0.06 m search radius and default k=20. Table 13 documents preparation costs, including 22 minutes per scene for GS optimization and 27.9 hours per dataset for teacher training. A project-page link replaces the future code-release statement, without establishing code availability from the PDFs alone.

E1.justification: v3 adds actual ScanNet200 instance-segmentation evaluation, extending coverage from semantic classification to grouping individual objects (Table 5). ScanNet v2, ScanNet200, ScanNet++, Matterport3D, and SceneSplat-7K remain represented. ScanNet200 hidden-test semantic evaluation was already present in v2.

E2.justification: For ScanNet v2, v3 Table 1 adds SPG and PT v3 + PPT and removes DeepViewAgg. For ScanNet200, v3 Table 2 adds PT v2, SPG, and PT v3 + PPT while removing OneFormer3D. Table 6 adds MinkUNet and OctFormer to the existing ScanNet++/Matterport3D comparisons. Table 5 adds instance-segmentation comparisons using MinkUNet, PT v2, and PT v3 backbones.

E3.justification: v3 introduces PointGroup-based instance evaluation with mAP25, mAP50, and mAP, plus new controlled protocols: boundary tests without distillation at fixed boundary-loss weight and attribute-distillation tests without the B–S block. Main semantic tables remove mAcc and several OA columns, although supplementary tables retain these metrics. Section 4.1 reports AdamW instead of v2's Adam; this reported setting revision does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond retained module and correspondence ablations, v3 tests semantic versus scale-based boundary supervision, appearance-encoder fine-tuning, individual Gaussian attributes and combinations, conventional-feature teachers, pruning ratios, loss weights, and class-group tradeoffs (Tables 8–9 and 14–17; Figure 11). Supplementary Sections B–D also add reconstruction-quality analysis, feature PCA visualizations, and boundary case studies.

E5.justification: Neither version reports random seeds, repeated-run counts, standard deviations, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The added scene-wise PSNR/mIoU comparison is descriptive analysis and does not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: G2P's core validation mIoUs remain 78.4, 36.6, 48.7, and 55.9 across the four semantic benchmarks. However, Table 4's hidden-test row changes from 35.5/55.3/28.6/18.7 to 35.7/54.3/28.7/20.2 for mIoU/Head/Common/Tail, making G2P highest on Tail. v3 adds instance results of 41.8 mAP25, 33.3 mAP50, and 23.2 mAP, plus extensive ablation and cost results. Several reproduced baseline scores are replaced by reference scores, and some secondary metric entries disappear; these replacements are not same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: Both versions retain Mahalanobis-weighted attribute aggregation, combined scale/semantic boundary labels, the Sonata teacher, PT v3 with the BFANet B–S block, and the same losses. Algorithm 1 and the clarified teacher inputs expand implementation documentation without establishing an algorithmic revision. The instance experiment uses G2P within a common PointGroup framework.

P1.justification: The main five-section organization and much of the prose remain. v3 revises the abstract, contribution wording, opacity terminology, method explanations, and ordering of experimental discussions. It also updates the title, authors, and affiliations and organizes the additional supplementary material into Sections A–E.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column formatting. v2's combined overview becomes separate preparation and training diagrams in v3 Figures 2 and 4, while Figure 3 is expanded. The existing qualitative comparison is retained as Figure 5. Tables are extensively restructured, including reduced metric columns and a transposed correspondence ablation, and numerous supplementary plots, tables, and qualitative panels are added.

R1.justification: The related-work organization and distinction from UniPre3D remain largely intact. v3 adds references including SPG, PT v2, PointGroup, Segment then Splat, DNGaussian, and Speedy-Splat, replaces the Bhattacharyya citation with Mahalanobis's distance paper, and removes the first-approach novelty wording. Publication and bibliographic updates to retained works are not additional research coverage.

T1.justification: The covariance, aggregation, boundary-selection, and loss definitions remain mathematically equivalent in Equations 1–9. Pruning-ratio notation is clarified, and pseudocode is supplied, but neither version introduces formal theorems or proofs, nor does v3 add a substantive mathematical derivation.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially improves the evidence supporting the individual Gaussian cues through boundary-source, teacher, and attribute controls that were absent from the supplied v2. Architecture, split, fallback, and preparation-cost disclosures make the approach more reproducible and its practical requirements assessable. More precise supervision claims and substantive limitations also improve credibility. These gains outweigh the loss of some secondary metric reporting; the assessment rests on stronger experimental support and documentation, rather than higher headline scores.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same G2P work, with matching core methods and experiments. All 11 pages of v2 and 33 pages of v3 were inspected, including rendered equations, tables, and figures. The supplied v2 ends with references; v3 additionally contains Supplementary Sections A–E.

after.justification: v3 retains original semantic-segmentation experiments and adds instance-segmentation results, attribute and boundary ablations, preparation-cost measurements, and supplementary analyses.

before.justification: v2 reports original G2P semantic-segmentation results, class-wise comparisons, ablations, and computational measurements in Tables 1–9.

results.title: G2P: Gaussian-to-Point Attribute Alignment for Boundary-Aware 3D Segmentation

C1.justification: v2 adds multi-institutional structured benchmark construction as a central contribution and extends the paper's claims to cross-institution generalization. It redefines the tokenization contribution around foreground-mask guidance and narrows patient-specific attribute extraction to localized lesion measurements. These changes materially extend and reshape v1's three-component, RadGenome-focused contribution statement.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations and limitations absent from v1: institutional reporting style can separate lexical from clinical scores; airway geometry may cause feature dilution; upstream segmentation misses constrain small-nodule detection; and organ-mask errors affect two visual modules, explaining their larger impact. These extend v1's discussion of component synergy and baseline behavior with explicit failure mechanisms and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v2 documents encoder layer selection, physical spacing, multi-window processing, DSPy/Llama-based report preparation, anatomical subregions, and revised lesion-extraction pseudocode. It updates context length from 2,048 to 8,192 and LoRA rank from 16 to 128, and supplies a concrete repository address where v1 only states code availability. Conversely, v1's explicit 48-hour/two-A100 baseline comparison cap is no longer documented.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates on RadGenome-Chest CT alone. v2 adds 500 AMC cases sampled from a separate hospital population and evaluates zero-shot cross-institution generalization, substantially expanding evaluation coverage while retaining the six-region chest reporting task.

E2.justification: The main comparison retains RadFM and M3D, removes MedBLIP and CT2Rep, and adds MedM-VL, Med3DVLM, and CT-CHAT (Table 1). The ablation comparison additionally introduces an M3D encoder baseline; the LITA comparator is retained under the LITAenc. label.

E3.justification: Reported training/validation and test counts change from 24,128/1,564 to 23,865/1,551. Inputs change from min-max-normalized 256×256×32 volumes to resampled, cropped, multi-window 448×448×128 inputs, and training increases from three to six epochs per stage. The clinical metric suite changes from CA-F1/GREEN/GPT-4 scoring to GREEN/CRG/GPT-CA. v2 also specifies 30% training subsets for ablations and introduces external zero-shot and 50-case blinded reader protocols.

E4.justification: v2 extends component ablations with encoder comparisons and external generalization tests, and adds analyses of anatomical-region weaknesses, nodule-size sensitivity, and organ-versus-lesion mask corruption (Tables S1, S3, S5). The earlier COVID-19 case is retained with revised outputs in Figure S1, while Figure 3 introduces a different multiregional effusion/consolidation case.

E5.justification: v1 provides point estimates without uncertainty reporting. v2 introduces 95% confidence intervals throughout the main comparison and ablation tables, specifies 10,000 bootstrap replicates, and reports reader-score standard deviations. These additions do not establish repeated training runs or increased seed counts.

E6.justification: The reported results are substantially replaced and expanded. For example, the proposed model's internal GREEN score is 0.278 in v1 and 0.4555 in v2, but changed methods and protocols prevent interpreting this as a controlled gain. New results include AMC GREEN 0.1572 and reader score 6.9792±1.4065. Table S3 also reveals small-nodule detection of 0.1270, below every listed baseline.

M1.justification: Beyond renaming R2 pooling, v2 replaces all-slice averaging and representative-slice selection with organ-bearing slice filtering and mask-guided spatial token selection. It replaces RAD-DINO/SAT with MedSigLIP/TotalSegmentator, removes spatial tokens, and produces one volumetrically pooled mask token per region. Attribute extraction changes from organ volumes and lesion counts/diameters to localized, largest-component lesion measurements (Sections 3.1–3.3; supplementary Algorithm 1).

P1.justification: The title and substantial portions of the abstract, introduction, related work, methods, and results discussion are rewritten. Related work is reorganized into three focused themes, structured reporting moves into a benchmark-construction subsection, component terminology changes, and the supplement is reorganized into dedicated implementation and analysis sections.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout. Figure 2 is substantially redrawn with separate tokenizer and attribute-extractor panels; baseline and ablation results become separate tables with confidence-interval rows; and supplementary Tables S1–S5 are added. The COVID-19 illustration is revised and relocated to Figure S1, while the main qualitative figure shows a new case.

Conversely, its amodal table omits v1's InternVL-3-38B, Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct, Qwen3-VL-32B-Thinking, and Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B-Instruct entries. The new component controls substantially expand the comparison methods beyond the original baseline comparisons.

E3.justification: V3 adds substantial control and diagnostic protocols: evaluating SFT-stage checkpoints, suppressing intermediate reasoning through a JSON schema, and tracking baseline failures using pre/post IoU bins. Failure attribution expands from GPT-4 alone to three model judges. These additions broaden the evaluation design; the retained benchmark splits, training budgets, and standard inference settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Unlike v1, v3 includes SFT/RL stage ablations, reasoning-suppression ablations across six models, and a hard-case recovery analysis in Appendices E–G. Appendix H expands failure analysis across judges and categories, while Figure 4 adds application case studies. The older Qwen qualitative examples are relocated, not newly introduced.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-training run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Dataset spread summaries and RL rollout sample counts are retained. The additional model judges extend the analysis design but are not presented as statistical uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Retained headline scores are unchanged, but v3 adds substantial results in Tables 9–12, including Qwen3-VL-8B EGM accuracy of 88.6 without reasoning versus 91.4 with it, and recovery of 3,030/6,082 hard cases. Gemini-3-Pro achieves 85.2 vanilla, 71.9 amodal, and 57.3 complex-subset accuracy. Some amodal results disappear. Section 5.3 also corrects gains to match retained tables, such as Qwen 2B's +5.5 becoming +6.0.

M1.justification: The reasoning-data pipeline, learnability-based RL sampling, SFT followed by GRPO, and reward remain unchanged. Renaming negative/positive samples to learnable/easy samples preserves the selection rules. Reasoning suppression is introduced as an experimental control, not a modification of the proposed EGM method.

P1.justification: The title, introductory framing, and RL-selection explanation are revised, including learnable/easy sample terminology. Existing Qwen qualitative discussion moves from Appendix C into new Section 5.6. Much of the earlier prose and section sequence is retained; the added scientific analyses account for much of the expansion.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to a single-column layout, with extensive resizing and repositioning of displays. V3 reorganizes the failure-subset and amodal tables, adds an RL-selection panel to Figure 3, introduces application demonstrations and analysis tables, and moves the existing Qwen qualitative figure into the main text.

R1.justification: V3 adds DROID and TARGO references supporting robotics examples and removes several background citations, including the original Qwen report and pix2gestalt. The overall positioning within grounding, amodal perception, and reasoning research remains, including the claim to first study amodal grounding in VLMs.

T1.justification: The grounding-success definition, learnability criterion, GRPO objective, advantage calculation, and reward equations remain substantively unchanged. Sample-set renaming is mathematically equivalent. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs; the new hard-sample bins concern empirical evaluation.

improvement.justification: V1 lacked direct component ablations despite attributing its gains to reasoning-based training. V3's Tables 9–10 supply training-stage and reasoning-suppression controls, while Tables 11–12 strengthen hard-case and failure-diagnosis evidence. These substantially improve assessment of the central mechanism without changing headline scores. Some amodal comparisons and generator-specific details are lost, and the controls do not fully establish the argument against distillation, but the added empirical scrutiny addresses an important evidential gap and provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Despite the changed title and layout, both PDFs describe the same EGM work, with matching methods and retained experiments. All 22 pages of v1 and 33 pages of v3, including Appendices A–D and A–H respectively, support comparison through readable text, equations, tables, and figures.

after.justification: V3 retains original grounding and efficiency results and adds component ablations, hard-sample analysis, additional model comparisons, and application demonstrations.

before.justification: V1 reports original EGM grounding experiments, failure-case analyses, qualitative predictions, and latency measurements, including Tables 1, 3–4 and Figure 4.

C1.justification: The panoramic-interface, ScanRefer/Nr3D performance and generalization claims remain. v2's introduction explicitly extends the applicability claim to casually captured RGB frames with off-the-shelf reconstruction. Its conclusion also omits v1's explicit open-vocabulary characterization.

C2.justification: v1's limitations paragraph mainly lists future tasks; v2 explicitly discusses reconstruction dependence, noise sensitivity and slower VLM inference. Added analyses explain ambiguous-reference, occlusion and partial-object failures, interpret backbone tradeoffs, and qualify the adapter design by finding exact mid/late placement noncritical (Appendices C–E).

D1.justification: v2 newly documents ground-truth initialization of the existing 3DGS variant, automatic reconstruction and checkpoint reuse, detailed QA supervision, smartphone capture specifications, 30K reconstruction steps, and stage-level CPU/GPU memory and timing. These substantially expand deployment and reproducibility information. The five-epoch training budget was already disclosed in v1.

E1.justification: v2 adds grounding under fully automated RGB-only reconstruction without ground-truth meshes or camera trajectories, plus a new self-captured living-room demonstration (Appendices C.1 and D.2). These substantially extend tested input conditions beyond the benchmark reconstructions in v1; the principal named benchmarks remain.

E2.justification: New Table 2 compares against ZSVG3D, SeeGround and VLM-Grounder in zero-shot Nr3D evaluation. Appendix D.1 adds LLaVA-3D to the resource comparison. Conversely, TSP3D is removed from Table 1. These change actual comparator participation, beyond citation or naming edits.

E3.justification: v2 restricts the representation comparison to 92 of 141 validation scenes, requiring at least 300 COLMAP-registered images, and evaluates automatic reconstructions with the existing 3DGS checkpoint. It also introduces zero-shot, smaller-backbone and linear-probe protocols. The text-variant table's metric changes from Acc@0.25 to Top-1, with unchanged values; this does not establish a rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds an all-feature control without EMD, inference-time geometry masking, adapter-layer ablations and linear probes, scene-size/category/elevation analyses, backbone scalability tests and explicit failure cases. Existing camera-placement, initialization, convergence and rotation analyses are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Appendix C.2 introduces a linear fit and correlation reporting for floor area versus camera count (r=0.80), adding a statistical estimation procedure absent from v1. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or formal significance tests.

E6.justification: Retained headline scores are unchanged, but v2 adds substantial results, including 53.2 zero-shot Nr3D accuracy and 52.1 ScanRefer accuracy with Qwen2.5-VL-7B. The representation comparison replaces v1's ScanRefer 3DGS/mesh scores of 59.3/61.0 with 60.8/61.6 on the restricted subset and adds automatic 3DGS at 55.1; these are not same-setting gains. Nr3D/Sr3D representation results are removed, while new diagnostic, resource and qualitative outcomes are added.

M1.justification: The stated geometric adapter band changes from [L/3,2L/3] to [L/3,2L/3), removing the shared endpoint with the semantic band (v1 Section 3.3; v2 Section 3.2). The core pipeline and objectives remain intact. Axis-based geometric QA was already documented in v1 Appendix A.4.

P1.justification: Substantial passages in the introduction, related work and method are rewritten. Panorama construction and adapters are merged into one subsection, benchmark discussion is consolidated, pinhole comparisons move under ablations, and the appendix is reorganized around analyses and deployment. Terminology and affiliations also change.

P2.justification: The paper changes from two-column to single-column layout, replaces the introductory overview, redraws pipeline and adapter diagrams, and adds numerous diagnostic and deployment displays. Two earlier appendix examples reappear in the introductory figure. The representation table is restructured, and existing mesh/3DGS images gain explanatory annotations.

R1.justification: v2 adds SpatialRGPT, COLMAP and visual-representation analysis citations while pruning works including SAT, LAR, ScanReason and TSP3D. Related work more explicitly contrasts curated 3D inputs, limited viewing coverage and specialized 3D tokens with PanoGrounder, while retaining the original central research positioning.

T1.justification: The camera-scoring, cross-view consistency, aggregation and weighted digit-EMD mathematics are retained. v2 explicitly writes the standard cross-entropy formula and clarifies notation, without adding a substantive derivation, theoretical assumption, theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for practical applicability and the contribution beyond a large backbone: it adds automatic reconstruction tests, a real capture demonstration, resource accounting, smaller-backbone comparisons and diagnostic controls. Concrete limitations and failure cases also improve transparency. The reconstruction comparison becomes narrower, excluding 49 validation scenes and dropping Nr3D/Sr3D representation results, while LIFT-GS retains its original evaluation setting. These limits constrain that comparison, but the added validation addresses important gaps in v1 and yields a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe PanoGrounder. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds zero-shot comparisons, reconstruction and deployment experiments, backbone evaluations and diagnostic analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original grounding experiments, cross-dataset and text generalization results, ablations, qualitative analyses and runtime measurements.

C1.justification: v2 emphasizes being the first multi-step spatial-reasoning benchmark and exploratory transfer to image generation. v4 recasts the contribution around Elementary and Planning sets, explicit plans through eight steps and multi-turn generation. Its abstract replaces the approximate half-accuracy ceiling with a remaining human gap and new claims of planning collapse, including zero accuracy for three-step generation.

C2.justification: v4 identifies incorrect step selection as a failure preceding ordering and discusses temporal and physical consistency requirements for generation. Appendix A attributes some human Height errors to insufficient attention; Appendix E argues that automatic judging reliably detects obvious failures but struggles with precise spatial judgments. v2's CoT and Qwen2.5-VL robustness interpretations are removed.

D1.justification: Appendices C–D newly provide eleven Elementary-task prompts, detailed task-specific scoring rubrics, annotator calibration and averaging procedures, and explanations of automatic versus human ground-truth construction. v4 also supplies identifiers for its new image-generation models. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation; the original project, code and dataset links remain.

E1.justification: The original 11 tasks become the Elementary set. v4 adds planning that requires selecting and ordering correct states among distractors, plus generating complete intermediate trajectories over multiple turns. These introduce distinct task requirements. v2's Next-k-Step scenario, selecting a state after adding specified pieces, is removed.

E2.justification: Table 1 expands from 20 to 29 models, adding GPT-5, GPT-o3, Gemini-2.5-Pro and Qwen3-VL/InternVL3/3.5 variants. Table 2 replaces five of six model comparators. The generation table adds GPT-5 and Nano Banana Pro and removes the numerical GPT-4o△ column, although that model's examples remain as GPT-4o* in the appendix. Planning generation also evaluates Nano Banana 2.

E3.justification: New planning VQA uses 20 cases per horizon, k correct and k distractor options, exact-match/set-match/overlap scoring and five human experts. Generation introduces topology-expanded valid trajectories, MSE matching and binary trajectory scoring. These differ substantially from v2's four-option Next-k-Step protocol with/without CoT. The generation sample count is inconsistent: 50 total cases versus 10 cases for each of four horizons.

E4.justification: v2's Next-k-Step/CoT ablation and its robustness findings are removed. v4 adds planning-error decomposition through exact versus set matching, human Height-error cases and an attention recheck, and human-versus-LLM judging analyses (Appendices A and E). Additional trajectory and single-turn generation cases expand the failure analysis.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run variability, seeds, confidence intervals or error bars. The random-guessing significance thresholds and cross-benchmark Pearson coefficients/p-values are retained. The new judge-agreement correlations and MAE/MSE values are evaluation results, without a new uncertainty-reporting procedure.

E6.justification: Shared Table 1 scores remain unchanged, including GPT-4o's 57.7%; v4 adds GPT-5 at 72.0% overall and 71.8% on Lite against humans' retained 93.6%. New planning results show GPT-5 exact match declining from 90% at k=1 to 0% at k=8, and all tested generators scoring zero at k=3–5. Next-k-Step/CoT results disappear, while appendix judge-agreement results are added.

M1.justification: Section 3.2.2 adds a turn-by-turn generation procedure in which each intermediate image is conditioned on previously generated states, extending v2's single-output generation setup. This is a limited inference-procedure adaptation; no new architecture, learned component or training objective is introduced, and the original curation pipeline remains.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and related-work narrative are extensively rewritten. Dataset definitions and experiments are reorganized around separate Elementary and Planning sets. The original image-generation evaluation moves into the discussion as an analysis of elementary generation failures, while dedicated appendix sections organize prompts, scoring guidance and case studies.

P2.justification: Figure 1 gains a planning example; the original Figure 2 is split, with a rearranged pipeline and the statistics chart moved to Appendix B. Comparison tables expand and reorder, the CoT table disappears, and new planning curves, trajectory panels, Height-error examples and judge-agreement tables are introduced. Generation grids are updated and expanded.

R1.justification: v4 replaces much of v2's reasoning-enhancement discussion with detailed positioning against spatial and planning benchmarks, including PhyBlock, ActPlan-1K, OrigamiSpace and GamiBench. It adds LEGO-related cognitive studies and newer-model references, and shifts novelty positioning toward challenging explicit planning and multi-turn generation.

T1.justification: Neither version develops theoretical results, proofs or substantive mathematical derivations. The added sequence notation, assembly-validity conditions and standard set-match/overlap scoring descriptions specify empirical tasks and protocols rather than introduce new mathematical theory.

improvement.justification: The new controlled planning tasks, human reference results and error decomposition substantially strengthen evidence for the central multi-step reasoning claims beyond v2's narrower tests. Elementary-task prompts, explicit scoring rubrics and evidence about automated judging also improve reproducibility and interpretation. These gains outweigh the loss of the CoT ablation and the unresolved generation sample-count inconsistency, which still weakens that experiment's reporting.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LEGO-Puzzles and retain matching original tasks and results. Text, tables and figures support comparison throughout. v2 ends with references and has no appendix; v4 includes readable Appendices A–G.

after.justification: v4 reports evaluations of 29 MLLMs, human comparisons, new planning experiments and image-generation results. Appendix E additionally reports original comparisons between GPT-4o judging and human ratings.

before.justification: v2 reports original evaluations of 20 MLLMs, human comparisons, image-generation experiments, Next-k-Step/CoT experiments and cross-benchmark correlations in Tables 1–5.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning spatial versus semantic reference cues, failures under large reference mismatch, and why medical segmentation baselines fail to select targets. It removes v1's qualification that specialized nnU-Net achieves better segmentation. Its new claim that LISA-SFT and SegZero-SFT degrade sharply on OOD data is not consistently supported by Table 3's scores across different datasets.

E1.justification: The benchmark datasets and modalities are retained; AMOS2022-MRI, CT-Liver, and CT-Lung already appeared in v1's Table 1. v2 adds a spatially shuffled-reference test scenario and an interactive annotation-refinement task, without establishing a new benchmark dataset.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds HuatuoGPT-Vision, Lingshu, MedRegA, BiRD, and MedPLIB. Table 3 adds MedSAM2-Memory, MedSAM2-Memory-Ref-SFT, LISA-SFT, and SegZero-SFT alongside retained SAM2 baselines. Added evaluations introduce ground-truth-box controls, shuffled references, LPIPS similarity bins, and a one-annotator study measuring time and clicks for 30 images containing 153 targets. Existing benchmark metrics and Table 1 training schedules remain.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained labeling-accuracy initialization ablation, v2 adds segmentation-metric ablations of VLM initialization/RL, oracle box prompting, and shuffled reference layouts in Table 5. Table S2 examines sensitivity to reference similarity, Figures S5–S6 show localization and segmentation failures, and Appendix C.6 investigates annotation effort.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The additional results retain point-estimate reporting; the annotation study's participant and image counts describe its evaluation sample.

E6.justification: Retained table entries remain numerically unchanged, but v2 adds substantial comparator, ablation, sensitivity, and annotation-cost results. For example, Table 5 reports RAOS Dice of 0.2088 with shuffled references versus 0.7151 for full RAU; Appendix C.6 reports 24.9 minutes versus nearly 250 for MedSAM2-Memory-Ref-SFT. Section 3.2 also revises its quoted RAOS comparison from 64.11% versus 78.16% to 74.68% versus 78.16%, using the retained RL-VQA baseline.

M1.justification: The Qwen/GRPO, global box-matching, and SAM2 architecture remains. However, v2's new experimental description and Appendix C.3 specify reference-image bounding boxes, conflicting with the target-image outputs described in v1 and retained in v2's Section 3.2. The PDFs do not resolve whether this reflects a procedure change or inconsistent documentation.

P1.justification: The introduction and related work are extensively rewritten, Section 3 gains a new explanatory roadmap, and method subsections separate methods, settings, and results. The conclusion is condensed, while the appendix is reorganized into datasets and task-specific experimental sections. These changes extend beyond accommodating new results.

P2.justification: v2 changes typography and page layout, expands Table 1, transposes and expands Table 3, and adds Table 5, Table S2, and failure-case Figures S5–S6. Figure 2 is reworked. Earlier Figures A1–A4 are retained as S3, S4, S1, and S2, respectively, with relocation and caption/layout edits rather than new qualitative evidence.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially reframes RAU against non-VLM clinical pipelines and medical VLM grounding, explicitly separating the reference-conditioned task from the algorithmic contribution. New medical-model, segmentation, retrieval, and clinical references broaden the positioning. The GLIP and SEEM citations also change from unrelated works in v1 to different grounding/segmentation papers.

Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs, and the new empirical analyses introduce no substantive mathematical development.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the empirical basis of RAU: broader medical-VLM and segmentation comparisons address v1's narrow comparator coverage, while shuffled-reference controls and reference-quality analyses directly examine the central spatial-reasoning claim and its failure boundaries. These gains outweigh the unresolved output/training inconsistencies, removal of the nnU-Net qualification, and unsupported blanket interpretation of OOD baseline deterioration.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RAU. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison despite extensive reformatting and supplementary-material reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, segmentation and reference-quality analyses, failure cases, and an annotation-cost study.
